model:claude|title:using a chaos loop to.content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. story|title:a background agent to fix br.content_excerpt: Use the GitHub Action arnaudrenaud/fix-with-agent to automatically fix your code whenever a dependency update breaks your test suite: Do you rely on a test suite that gives you enough confidence to blindly merge pull requests from automatic dependency update bots such as Dependabot or Renovate? If so, you’re already saving time compared to manual updates and regression testing. Yet, you may still be sitting on a backlog of unmerged pull requests because of breaking changes following major updates (and even, sometimes, minor ones…). Now that AI helps attackers exploit vulnerabilities faster, you’d better have AI help you patch them as soon as possible and keep up with major version upgrades over the years. Of course, pulling the faulty branch and asking your local agent to “fix tests following dependency update” should do the trick with little supervision. Still, the operation induces friction: Let’s automate everything but the last two steps: reviewing and merging will remain up to you. There is no need to orchestrate our agent manually when its boundaries can be defined as follows: Here is an example of workflow for a Node.js, NPM-managed project: it fixes failing tests in Renovate pull requests using action arnaudrenaud/fix-with-agent . With this workflow, if your test suite fails following a Renovate pull request and the agent manages to fix it, you’ll see the following changes in the pull request: a comment has been published, reporting obstacles encountered and decisions taken (the same report is mentioned in the commit body and action output): Here is only one example of a small, circumscribed task that can be completed with an autonomous background agent. Let’s take the time to spot the recurring, well-defined tasks that can be performed on the side either on a fixed schedule or following a specific event. This way, we’ll clear not only the core of the task, but also the mental load of getting notified and making time for it.

The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage. For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work. A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review." Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found. story|title:linux sandboxes from s3 93 9.content_excerpt: Your AI agent runs untrusted code. One pip install gives you hardware-isolated VMs. No cloud account, no API key, no egress fees. exec-sandbox runs untrusted Python, JavaScript or shell code in QEMU microVMs on your own Linux or macOS hosts, for example code that an AI agent wrote. It is a Python asyncio library with a command line ( sbx ). It needs no cloud account and no API key. The other Python examples use async with and await at the top level: run them in an async def function, as main() above. With pip, use pip install with the same names. For sbx with the s3 store, install exec-sandbox[cli,s3] . exec-sandbox uses qemu-system-x86_64 or qemu-system-aarch64 from /usr/bin/ , else from PATH ( EXEC_SANDBOX_QEMU_BIN_X86 and EXEC_SANDBOX_QEMU_BIN_ARM set another file), and qemu-img and qemu-storage-daemon from PATH . A missing QEMU binary, or one whose version or machine types this user cannot read, raises ConfigError ( HOST_DEPENDENCY ) when the Scheduler starts; a missing qemu-img raises it at its first use. Check the version with /usr/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 --version (or qemu-system-aarch64 ): Ubuntu 24.04 ships 8.2.2. Saved instances and L1 snapshots need QEMU 11.0 or later: where the distribution ships an older one, build QEMU from its source release ( qemu.org/download ) and set EXEC_SANDBOX_QEMU_BIN_X86 or EXEC_SANDBOX_QEMU_BIN_ARM to the binary. On Linux, give your user access to KVM with sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER , then log in again. Without this access, exec-sandbox logs a warning and uses TCG. To run QEMU as its own user, with cgroup limits and namespaces, see Linux host setup . The first run downloads the VM images ( How images download ). For Python, see the example at the top and Sessions . sbx comes with the cli extra; all its options are in the CLI reference . scheduler.new(spec) starts a new VM and returns its session. The session keeps variables, imports, files and background processes between exec() calls ( Limits ), until close() destroys the VM. Some errors close a session ( What closes a session ). JavaScript sessions (also TypeScript) keep variables and functions. Shell sessions ( raw , Bash) keep environment variables, the working folder and functions. A session closes after session_idle_timeout_seconds (default 300) with no call. For one session, pass idle_timeout_seconds (10-3600) to new() or reuse() ; a value out of range raises InvalidInputError ( ARGUMENT_INVALID ). story|title:shard distributed ai inferen.content_excerpt: Local LLM inference engine with pre-flight model fit checks, GGUF/PyTorch backends, OpenAI-compatible API, and LAN VRAM pooling (experimental P2P/WAN relay) One Network. Many Servers. Shared AI Infrastructure. Distributed local LLM inference engine pooling GPU VRAM and system RAM across LAN machines — powered by PyTorch, FastAPI, llama.cpp RPC, and native C++20 / MASM AVX2 SIMD kernels. SHARD Distributed Inference Cluster: Central master coordinator pooling VRAM across connected LAN worker nodes over UDP discovery ( :8001 ) and FastAPI SSE endpoints ( :8000 ). Overview · How It Works · Features · Quick Start · CLI Reference · Architecture · Dashboard · Community SHARD ( shard-engine ) is an open-source distributed local LLM inference engine written in Python ( FastAPI + PyTorch ) with a GGUF / llama.cpp backend and native C++20 / MASM AVX2 SIMD acceleration. Running capable 14B, 32B, or 70B+ open-weight language models locally typically hits a hard hardware wall: single-card VRAM limits . Most developers, labs, and small teams own multiple machines—a desktop gaming GPU, a workstation laptop, an auxiliary mini-PC—whose memory sits fragmented across the local network while no single device can fit the full model weights and KV cache. SHARD unites idle GPUs and system memory across your Local Area Network (LAN) into a single logical inference cluster: SHARD turns distributed local AI infrastructure into a four-step workflow: CREATE → SHARE → CONNECT → USE . Start a local SHARD node with shard start or python main.py . The engine probes your CPU, system RAM, and NVIDIA CUDA / Apple MPS GPU via hardware.py , loads your chosen GGUF or Hugging Face model, and brings up the FastAPI server and Web UI on http://localhost:8000 . Open a LAN compute pool with shard lan create --open (or generate a pairing code via shard lan create ). SHARD broadcasts UDP discovery beacons on port 8001 and exposes /api/lan/* endpoints so peer machines on your subnet can pool their VRAM and RAM. On any secondary computer on the network, run shard lan join <master-ip> --share . The worker completes an HTTP handshake ( POST /api/lan/pair ), launches its local RPC tensor worker, sends periodic health heartbeats, and contributes its GPU/RAM to the cluster. Connect coding IDEs, autonomous AI agents, or custom Python apps to http://<master-ip>:8000/v1/chat/completions or /v1/messages . story|ver:7.5|title:how we raised databr.content_excerpt: Why adaptive concurrency limits work better than fixed request-rate limits for long-running operations. As part of the Compute Platform team at Databricks, we turn cloud infrastructure into clusters ready to run customer workloads. Our day-to-day work includes provisioning virtual machines and coordinating cluster creation across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Our goal is to keep these systems available while letting customers use as much capacity as we can safely provide. In this post, we'll explore why fixed request-rate limits can fall short for these long-running operations, how adaptive concurrency limits help, and what we learned applying them to cluster creation for Databricks classic compute. You don't need to know any of this to use Databricks, but if you're curious about what happens behind a Databricks Runtime cluster launch, join us for a look inside the kitchen. Historically, we protected the system with fixed request-rate limits, tested against different load patterns and failure scenarios. We scaled our services primarily by adding resources and adjusting per-customer limits. The combination of workloads and dependency failures made these limits increasingly difficult to test and tune. Conservative limits turned away customer requests despite spare capacity, yet kept accepting requests when our services or dependencies, such as cloud providers, slowed down. Engineers manually lowered limits to shed load during incidents and raised them again after recovery. Adaptive concurrency limits account for both unfinished work and changing system health. They let more work start when capacity is available and slow the pace when the system struggles, helping the service make progress with less manual tuning. A fixed API request-rate ceiling remains as a final safety guardrail against exceptionally high incoming traffic. Think of our compute platform as a kitchen, aiming to serve as many orders as its cooks and equipment can handle. The manager posts a fixed rule: accept at most ten new orders per minute, whatever is happening at the stove. Even with spare cooking capacity, the rule turns orders away. When an oven breaks, it keeps accepting orders faster than the remaining cooks and equipment can finish them. The manager has to keep rewriting the sign each time.
